text: Last lesson you turned a vague request into a specific requirement. This lesson turns that requirement into a plan — what the Bronze, Silver, and Gold layers will each actually hold, in plain English, before you write a single line of real PySpark.

Here's the plan. Bronze, the table bronze dot daily sales raw, holds the daily extract exactly as it arrives — no cleaning, no casting, no deduplication, whatever columns the source happens to have. Silver, silver dot sales transactions, holds one row per sale line item, cleaned: duplicates removed, dates and amounts cast to real types, and both the in-store and online shapes unified into one. Gold, gold dot daily sales summary, holds exactly what lesson one asked for — one row per calendar day, with that day's total sales and order count.

Drawn out, it's a straight line: Bronze feeds Silver through deduplication and type casting and dropping bad rows, and Silver feeds Gold through a group-by on date with a sum and a count. Three short definitions, written down now, instead of discovered halfway through writing code later.

One more decision worth naming: every one of these three layers is a Delta table, not just a folder of files. That buys you a transaction log — schema enforcement so a bad column doesn't silently corrupt Silver, time travel back to a previous version, and MERGE support, which is what lets a future version of this pipeline update Silver and Gold incrementally instead of rebuilding from scratch every single run.
That's the whole plan for this pipeline. Next lesson, you'll write the first real PySpark: reading the raw sales extract and landing it, completely untouched, as the Bronze Delta table.
